title: IRDAI Sets Up a Seven-Member Working Group to Draft India's First AI Governance Framework for Insurance, With a Three-Month Deadline
summary: On June 19, 2026 IRDAI announced a seven-member working group, chaired by IIIT Hyderabad's Sandeep K. Shukla, to map AI use in insurance and propose a framework for ethical, transparent and explainable AI, with recommendations due in three months; they will not automatically become binding rules.
description:
India's insurance regulator has started work on rules for artificial intelligence in insurance. According to a report in Insurance Business Asia, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) announced on June 19, 2026 that it had set up a seven-member working group to examine how AI is used in the sector and to propose a governance framework. The group has three months to deliver recommendations, which the report says are expected to form the basis of the sector's first formal AI governance framework. The recommendations, however, will not automatically become binding regulation.

The group is chaired by Sandeep K. Shukla, director of the International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad. Its membership combines technology security and insurance experience. It includes serving and former senior officials from CERT-In, India's computer emergency response team, and from Reserve Bank Information Technology (ReBIT), a technology arm of the Reserve Bank of India, along with representatives from a life insurer, a general insurer and a standalone health insurer. Deepak Gaikwad, IRDAI's general manager and chief information security officer, is the member convener.

The mandate is broad. The group is to map current AI adoption among regulated entities, including the systems in use and the existing governance structures around them. It is to propose a framework for ethical, transparent and explainable AI, with a focus on claims processing and fraud detection. Those two areas are where an automated decision can directly affect a policyholder: whether a claim is paid, delayed or flagged as suspicious. The group is also to assess the effect of frontier AI tools on insurance operations, prescribe security controls against AI-driven automated attacks, and examine whether stress tests are needed for AI-related failures.

Further items concern oversight. The group will review how other markets supervise AI in insurance, develop an audit framework covering pre- and post-deployment requirements, and identify skills gaps and capacity-building needs. The report notes that the audit framework could help clarify who is responsible when AI makes an error in claims or fraud decisions, a question for which no framework currently exists in India. That question of accountability recurs in discussions of AI in insurance: if an algorithm wrongly rejects a claim, it is not obvious whether responsibility lies with the insurer, the vendor that built the model or the person who approved its use.

The group follows IRDAI's revised information and cyber security guidelines, issued in April 2026, which require compliance during the current financial year. The report says the working group's recommendations will not automatically become binding regulation, meaning IRDAI would need to take a further step, such as issuing guidelines or regulations, after considering them.

The report adds industry context from GlobalData. A poll of 113 insurance respondents in the first half of 2026 found that close to a quarter believed AI was not yet ready for widespread use in insurance. GlobalData analyst Ben Carey-Evans linked this to limited use cases so far and unresolved liability, saying that "there is concern around who is liable for mistakes made by AI." GlobalData also recorded about 63,293 active insurance AI-related job listings worldwide in 2025, an increase of roughly 50.9% from 2024, which suggests that hiring is growing even as concerns remain.

How does this compare with other regulators? Singapore's regulator has published draft guidelines on AI risk management, proposed in November 2025, and in July 2026 released an industry white paper on runtime safeguards for AI agents. India's approach, a working group that reports within three months, is a first step rather than a final rule. The group's mandate to review other markets suggests it will draw on such examples, but the report does not say which jurisdictions it will study.

Timing is worth noting. A three-month deadline from the June 19 announcement points to recommendations around the end of September 2026. The report available for this article does not say whether the group has delivered, and the sources reviewed contain no later reports, so the status of the recommendations is unknown. Readers should check IRDAI's website for any published outcome or any consultation that follows.

For insurers, the working group is a signal to prepare. Companies using AI for claims triage, underwriting or fraud detection may wish to inventory their systems, document how models are trained and tested, set up human review for adverse decisions, and strengthen security against AI-assisted attacks. For policyholders, the main potential benefit is clarity about how automated decisions are made and who can be held to account. For technology vendors, the audit framework may bring new requirements for documentation and testing.

The limitations of the report should be kept in mind. It describes a mandate, not results. It does not say how often the group meets, whether it will consult the public or what form the final framework would take. Until IRDAI publishes the recommendations and decides what to adopt, the situation remains one of expectations rather than rules.
source_name: Insurance Business Asia (IRDAI AI working group report, June 2026)
image_alt: Artificial intelligence governance in insurance technology India (illustrative)
key_points: IRDAI announced a seven-member working group on June 19, 2026, chaired by Sandeep K. Shukla, director of the International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad, with three months to deliver recommendations.

Members include serving and former senior officials from CERT-In and Reserve Bank Information Technology (ReBIT) and representatives of a life insurer, a general insurer and a standalone health insurer; IRDAI's chief information security officer Deepak Gaikwad is member convener.

The mandate includes mapping AI adoption, proposing a framework for ethical, transparent and explainable AI focused on claims processing and fraud detection, assessing frontier AI tools, prescribing security controls against AI-driven attacks and considering stress tests for AI failures.
The group is also to develop a pre- and post-deployment audit framework, review how other markets supervise AI in insurance, and identify skills gaps.

The recommendations are expected to form the basis of the sector's first formal AI governance framework but will not automatically become binding regulation; a GlobalData poll found close to a quarter of 113 insurance respondents believed AI was not yet ready for widespread use.
why_it_matters: Indian insurers are using AI for claims and fraud detection, decisions that can decide whether a family gets paid. The working group's work could set the first rules on explainability, accountability and testing for those systems.

title: London's Heat Ready Plan Puts the Cost of Making the Most Vulnerable Homes Resilient at £9 Billion to £45 Billion, as Khan Says the Costs of Inaction Outweigh Action
summary: London Mayor Sadiq Khan's heat resilience plan says making the most vulnerable homes resilient would cost between £9 billion and £45 billion, against £1.5 billion in costs from the 2022 heatwaves, with private investment needed and insurers such as Swiss Re and Zurich framing heat as a risk that amplifies other losses.
description:
London's mayor has put a price on preparing the capital's homes for extreme heat, and the figure is large. According to a Bloomberg report published by Insurance Journal on June 25, 2026, the city's heat resilience plan, which the article calls Heat Ready London, estimates that making the most vulnerable homes resilient would cost between £9 billion and £45 billion. By comparison, the heatwaves of 2022 cost London £1.5 billion, or about $2 billion. The wide range reflects uncertainty over how many homes and what measures are included, and the article does not explain how the two ends of the range were built. Other details sometimes quoted in coverage of the plan, such as particular alert levels or monthly record temperatures, are not in this source and are left out.

The numbers

The plan says private investment will be needed, since public funds alone are unlikely to cover a bill of that scale. About one million homes in London are at high risk of overheating, according to the report. Mayor Sadiq Khan said that the costs of inaction outweigh the cost of action. Simple arithmetic shows how the numbers compare: £9 billion is six times the £1.5 billion cost of the 2022 heatwaves, and £45 billion is thirty times, so the argument depends on heatwaves recurring and growing in severity over many years, which the article implies but does not quantify.

The heat itself

The report describes temperatures around 35C in London. Greenpeace recorded more than 55C on pavements and platforms, a figure that reflects surface heat in direct sun and not air temperature. London Ambulance Service logged 642 Category 1 calls on the Wednesday, the highest number it has ever recorded for a day. Category 1 is the most urgent category, for life-threatening conditions. The article does not report any heat deaths and does not say how many of the calls were related to heat. That is an important qualification: the call volume is consistent with heat stress, but the report does not establish the cause of each call.

What the plan proposes

The plan lists priorities including external shutters, shade, trees, access to swimming, cooler schools and air conditioning for vulnerable settings. These are a mix of passive measures, such as shade and shutters, which reduce indoor temperatures without using energy, and active cooling for places that care for vulnerable people. The emphasis on schools and vulnerable settings reflects the people most at risk, such as children, older residents and those with health conditions. The article does not give a breakdown of the cost by measure.

The insurance angle

The report links the plan to insurance. Swiss Re Institute calls heat a risk amplifier, meaning that heat does not only cause direct damage but also makes other risks worse, for example by stressing power grids, damaging infrastructure, harming health and raising the chances of fire. Linda Freiner of Zurich spoke about pricing resilience, which refers to the question of whether insurers can reflect the benefits of resilience measures in the prices they charge. If a building has shutters, shade and cooling, an insurer might regard it as a better risk, but the report does not describe any actual pricing scheme.

The report also notes that Switzerland is warming more than twice as fast as the global average and that French minister Éléonore Caroit said buildings were not designed for these temperatures. Those remarks put London's problem into a European context: much of the building stock in northern Europe was designed for cooler climates.

Who pays

The estimated bill raises the question of who pays for retrofitting homes. Many vulnerable homes are rented or owned by people with limited means, and the plan says private investment will be needed. The article does not describe any financing mechanism, so it is not clear whether the money would come from landlords, lenders, insurers or grants. Insurers and reinsurers have a role as investors and as risk assessors, but the report does not say they will fund the programme.

What to take from it

The plan's central claim is economic: spending on resilience now is cheaper than paying for the consequences of repeated heatwaves. The range of £9 billion to £45 billion shows how uncertain the cost is. For insurers, the message is that heat is a growing risk worth modelling. For homeowners and landlords, it is a signal that cooling and shading measures may become more valuable. For policymakers, it highlights the need for funding models.

Questions the report leaves open

Several questions cannot be answered from the article. It does not say how many homes make up the group of the most vulnerable, so the cost per home cannot be calculated. It does not state the time frame over which the £9 billion to £45 billion would be spent. It does not explain how the 2022 cost of £1.5 billion was calculated, for example whether it includes health costs, lost productivity or damage to property. And it does not say how much of the cost insurers could be expected to bear. These gaps matter because the argument that action is cheaper than inaction depends on the frequency of future heatwaves and on how long the measures last.

For insurers, the story is a reminder that heat is a risk that spreads through other lines of business, such as health, property, business interruption and infrastructure. For residents, the practical measures, shade, shutters and ventilation, are known and relatively simple; the challenge identified in the plan is scale and funding.

Limits

This article summarises a news report of the plan and not the plan itself, and it contains no data on health outcomes or costs per measure. It is general information, not insurance or planning advice.

key_points: The 2022 heatwaves cost London £1.5 billion ($2 billion), and making the most vulnerable homes resilient would cost £9 billion to £45 billion, with private investment needed.
Mayor Sadiq Khan said the costs of inaction outweigh the cost of action, and about 1 million London homes are at high risk of overheating.

Temperatures were around 35C, Greenpeace recorded more than 55C on pavements and platforms, and London Ambulance Service logged 642 Category 1 calls on a Wednesday, its highest ever; the article reports no heat deaths.
The plan's priorities include external shutters, shade, trees, swimming access, cooler schools and air conditioning for vulnerable settings.
Swiss Re Institute calls heat a risk amplifier, and Zurich's Linda Freiner spoke about pricing resilience, framing the issue as one for insurers as well as for city planners.
why_it_matters: Heat is usually less visible in insurance figures than floods or storms, but it affects health, infrastructure and property. A city estimating a bill in the tens of billions for housing alone shows why resilience financing, and insurers' view of it, is becoming part of climate planning.

title: Allianz: Global Insurance Premiums Grew 7.1% to €6.9 Trillion in 2025, With Health the Fastest Segment and Asia Set to Drive the Next Decade
summary: Allianz Research says global insurance premiums rose 7.1% to €6.9 trillion in 2025, adding €456 billion; health premiums jumped 12.3%, life rose 6.9% and P&C 3.8%, and it forecasts 5.3% annual growth over ten years with wider Asia adding more than North America and Western Europe combined.
description:
The world insurance industry grew faster than most economies in 2025, according to Allianz Research. In the Allianz Global Insurance Report 2026, titled "The Future of Insurance in a Fragmenting World" and published on May 28, 2026 by the research team of Allianz Investment Management SE, the group estimates that global insurance premiums grew 7.1% to €6.9 trillion in 2025. That added €456 billion of premiums in a single year. Growth slowed from 9.4% in 2024, but it remained above the ten-year average of 5.6%.

The three main segments grew at different speeds. Life premiums reached €2,861 billion, P&C (property and casualty) premiums €2,320 billion, and health premiums €1,688 billion. Health was the standout, with premiums up 12.3%, the fastest growth since 2014. In North America health premiums grew 14.9%, and the report says the United States accounts for over 70% of global health premiums. In Asia, health insurance penetration, meaning premiums relative to the size of the economy, is below 1% in almost all markets, so the report sees substantial room to grow.

P&C premiums rose 3.8%, compared with 8.5% in 2024, as pricing cycles matured. North America holds 52% of global P&C premiums but grew only 2.2%, while Western Europe grew 5.3% and Asia 4.0%. The slowdown in North America matches other data: Marsh's index shows US composite commercial rates down only 1% in the third quarter of 2026 after rising sharply in earlier years, and AM Best has reported a $16.5 billion US homeowners underwriting profit for 2025, signalling that price increases are no longer as large.

Life premiums rose 6.9%, down from 11.3% in 2024. The report says the annuity boom in North America is losing momentum. Asia grew 9.9% in life premiums, with China up 11.4%. These patterns reflect the effect of interest rates: high rates made annuities attractive in the United States in 2023 and 2024, and the surge is now fading, while Asian growth is driven by rising incomes and demand for savings and protection.

The report looks ahead ten years, to 2036. Allianz forecasts overall market growth of 5.3% a year, slightly above economic output. By segment, it expects P&C to grow 4.7% a year, life 4.9% and health 6.7%. The total premium pool is projected to increase by €5,260 billion, including €1,991 billion for life, €1,505 billion for P&C and €1,764 billion for health. The geography of that growth is the key theme. Wider Asia adds €1,004 billion, more than North America (€416 billion) and Western Europe (€402 billion) combined. North America keeps about 46% of global market share, down 0.5 percentage points, while India and China together gain almost 4 percentage points. Western Europe loses about 4 percentage points, following a loss of 5.3 points over the last decade. The page reviewed gives ten-year figures to 2036.

The report's title refers to fragmentation, and the authors discuss what it means for insurers. Geopolitical fragmentation weakens cross-border business models and diversification, which are central to global insurers and reinsurers, but it also raises demand for resilience and specialised cover such as political risk and energy security. The report says that "resilience is replacing efficiency as the dominant organizing principle," a shift it links to the need for affordability. In practice, this suggests customers and governments will pay more attention to whether risks are covered and claims are paid in a crisis, and less to the lowest cost. The page reviewed does not detail specific products or policies in response.

A simple calculation from the segment figures shows the mix of the market. The three segments sum to about €6,869 billion, so life accounts for roughly 42% of global premiums, P&C about 34% and health about 25%. Because health is growing fastest, both in 2025 and in the forecast, its share should rise, although the report summary reviewed does not state a target share. The forecast increases are also informative: of the €5,260 billion of additional premiums expected over ten years, life contributes about 38%, P&C about 29% and health about 34%, meaning health is expected to supply a third of new premiums from a quarter of today's base. These shares are the author's arithmetic from the published figures, not statements in the report.

The authors are Michaela Grimm, Patrick Hoffmann, Simon Krause, Hazem Krichene, Kathrin Stoffel and Katharina Utermöhl. The report is a research publication from the insurer's own economists, and it should be read as one respected view, not as an official statistic. Allianz is itself a major global insurer with interests in the trends it describes, such as its recent agreement to buy HSBC's Singapore life insurer, an example of the Asian expansion the report highlights.

What are the implications? For insurers, the report supports a strategy of looking to Asia, especially India and China, and to health insurance, where growth is fastest and penetration low. For regulators, it points to the need to supervise fast-growing markets and to manage risks from geopolitical fragmentation. For consumers, the growth of health premiums, 12.3% in a year, reflects rising healthcare costs and demand, and in the United States, where most of the premium is, it coincides with concerns about affordability.

Several figures are not in the material reviewed, including wealth figures and general insurance penetration measures beyond the Asian health figure. Readers who need those should consult the full PDF report from Allianz Research.
source_name: Allianz Research (Allianz Global Insurance Report 2026, published May 28, 2026)
image_alt: Global insurance industry growth and premium market analysis (illustrative)
key_points: Global insurance premiums grew 7.1% to €6.9 trillion in 2025, adding €456 billion; growth slowed from 9.4% in 2024 but stayed above the ten-year average of 5.6%.
By segment, life premiums were €2,861 billion (up 6.9%), P&C €2,320 billion (up 3.8%) and health €1,688 billion (up 12.3%, the fastest since 2014).
North America holds 52% of global P&C premiums but grew only 2.2%; Asia's life premiums grew 9.9%, with China up 11.4%, and the US accounts for over 70% of global health premiums.

Allianz forecasts 5.3% annual premium growth over ten years, adding €5,260 billion in total, with wider Asia contributing €1,004 billion, more than North America (€416 billion) and Western Europe (€402 billion) combined.

The report says geopolitical fragmentation weakens cross-border diversification but raises demand for resilience and specialised cover, adding that 'resilience is replacing efficiency as the dominant organizing principle.'
why_it_matters: This is the most comprehensive annual measure of the size and direction of the world insurance market. It shows where growth is coming from, why prices and demand are shifting, and why insurers are looking to Asia and health products for expansion.

title: ICICI Lombard Becomes Lloyd's Local Partner in India, Issuing Local Policies for Multinational Programmes Across 13 Classes of Business
summary: Lloyd's announced on June 18, 2026 that ICICI Lombard General Insurance will issue local policies in India on behalf of Lloyd's managing agents for selected lines, adding to Lloyd's existing routes into the market through cross-border reinsurance, Lloyd's India and its GIFT City platform.
description:
Lloyd's of London has added a local partner in India, and the arrangement shows how a global specialty market reaches a country that regulates insurance closely. In a news item dated June 18, 2026, Lloyd's said that ICICI Lombard General Insurance Company Ltd will act as its local partner in India. Under the arrangement, the Lloyd's page states, "ICICI Lombard will issue local policies on behalf of managing agents for selected lines of business." Business Insurance reported the agreement on June 22, 2026, crediting Asia Insurance Post, and Intelligent Insurer carried the story on June 19 under the heading "Lloyd's enhances India access with local partnership."

To see why a local partner matters, it helps to understand multinational insurance. A company with operations in several countries often wants one programme that gives consistent cover across all of them. In many markets, however, the law requires that insurance covering local risks be issued by a locally authorised insurer, so the global policy has to be matched by a local one in each country. Lloyd's is not itself an insurer but a marketplace of syndicates run by managing agents, so in markets with such rules it signs local partners who can issue the local policy while Lloyd's syndicates carry the risk. Lloyd's says it already delivers multinational programmes and local policies in more than 80 territories, and that its reinsurance capabilities reach more than 200 countries and territories.

The mechanics, as Lloyd's describes them, are simple. A managing agent that wants a local policy in India submits the request through Lloyd's Multinational team, which works with ICICI Lombard and arranges the documentation. Lloyd's keeps oversight of performance, premium collection, claims handling and policy issuance. Managing agents pay no additional fee for the arrangement. The Lloyd's announcement does not say which regulatory framework the arrangement relies on, does not name the specific lines covered in the news item itself, and does not give premium or volume expectations, so none of those should be assumed.

A separate Lloyd's guidance document for India fills in more of the picture. It lists 13 classes of business: property, engineering, miscellaneous, marine cargo, marine hull, liability, aviation, travel, group personal accident, group health insurance, terrorism, energy and trade credit. It also describes three ways in which Lloyd's underwriters can reach the Indian market. They can continue to reinsure Indian business cross-border from hubs such as London. Managing agents can set up a service company on the Lloyd's India platform to act as an onshore reinsurer. Or they can set up a service company on Lloyd's GIFT City platform, using the licence Lloyd's has newly authorised there. The ICICI Lombard partnership supports the Multinational offering, which the document says provides multinational insurance solutions that comply with local regulatory frameworks, and the Multinational team acts as a knowledge partner between managing agents and ICICI Lombard and provides on-demand support. The aim, in Lloyd's words, is to widen access and options for firms delivering global insurance and reinsurance solutions.

ICICI Lombard's role carries both an opportunity and a responsibility. The partner issues the local policy and Lloyd's syndicates take the underlying risk, so the partner needs systems, compliance and claims handling that meet Indian requirements, while Lloyd's underwriters supply capacity that a single local insurer might not want to retain. ICICI Lombard is one of India's larger private general insurers, but the announcements do not give financial details of the arrangement, and none should be inferred.

The timing is linked to a broader opening of the Indian market. The Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025 was passed by Parliament in December 2025 and, after the President's assent, the government notified February 5, 2026 as the enforcement date for most of its provisions. Outlook Business reported on February 12, 2026 that the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, under the Commerce and Industry Ministry, issued Press Note 1 (2026 Series) amending the consolidated FDI policy. It allows 100% foreign investment in insurance companies under the automatic route, while for the Life Insurance Corporation of India only 20% is permitted under the automatic route. In an Indian insurance company with foreign investment, at least one of the chairperson, managing director or chief executive officer must be a resident Indian citizen. The previous ceiling was 74%.

The local partner arrangement does not itself depend on foreign ownership, because Lloyd's is not buying an Indian insurer. What the liberalisation did was change the setting in which global groups think about India, as both an investment and a source of specialty business. For Lloyd's, which already has a reinsurance presence through Lloyd's India and its platform in GIFT City, a local partner adds a way to serve clients who need a locally issued policy.

For Indian businesses the benefits, if they come, will be indirect. A company with subsidiaries abroad that buys a global programme from a Lloyd's broker can have the Indian leg issued locally, which saves it from separate negotiations with Indian insurers for those risks. A company that is only domestic would see little change, apart from possible additional capacity in specialty lines. The unknowns are important: how many managing agents will use the route, how much premium will flow through it, and how it will be received by the regulator over time. For now, the record is an agreement, the process Lloyd's has set out, and a list of classes, not a measure of results.
source_name: Lloyd's (June 18, 2026), Business Insurance (June 22, 2026) and Intelligent Insurer (June 19, 2026)
image_alt: India insurance market globalization and international partnership (illustrative)
key_points: Lloyd's announced on June 18, 2026 that ICICI Lombard General Insurance Company will act as its local partner in India, issuing local policies on behalf of managing agents for selected lines of business.

Managing agents request local policies through Lloyd's Multinational team, which works with ICICI Lombard on documentation; Lloyd's keeps oversight of performance, premium collection, claims handling and policy issuance, at no additional cost to managing agents.

Lloyd's lists 13 classes in its India local partner guidance, including property, engineering, marine cargo and hull, liability, aviation, travel, group personal accident, group health, terrorism, energy and trade credit.

The partnership sits alongside other routes: cross-border reinsurance from hubs such as London, a service company on the Lloyd's India platform acting as an onshore reinsurer, and a service company on Lloyd's GIFT City platform.

It follows India's move to allow 100% foreign direct investment in insurance companies under the automatic route, notified in Press Note 1 (2026 Series) and reported on February 12, 2026; it was not a May 2026 notification.
why_it_matters: Multinational companies that operate in India need insurance that is valid under Indian rules, and global specialty markets such as Lloyd's can only sell it through an arrangement the regulator accepts. A local partner issues the policy on the ground while Lloyd's underwriters carry the risk behind it, which makes it easier for an international client to buy one programme covering many countries. For India it is a sign that global insurers are building structures for the market after the foreign-investment limit was lifted. For Indian businesses the effect will be gradual: more global specialty capacity can be offered locally without each insurer having to set up a branch.
